content: 1. Implementation of Improved CTG Technology: Women giving birth in settings with high-quality maternity care may benefit from advancements in cardiotocography (CTG) technology. This includes exploring the feasibility and cost-effectiveness of intermittent CTG use in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) and comparing its outcomes with intermittent auscultation (IA) using Doppler ultrasound devices. 2. Opioid Analgesia in Labor: Research is needed to understand women’s values and experiences regarding opioid use for pain relief during labor. Additionally, the potential association between intrapartum opioid use and subsequent opioid dependency in offspring should be investigated. 3. Episiotomy Policy in the Second Stage of Labor: For women in the second stage of labor, selective episiotomy based on clearly defined clinical indications may improve birth outcomes compared to no episiotomy. This requires further evaluation. 4. 5. Guideline Dissemination: The WHO intrapartum care guideline will be made available online and in print. It will be accessible through the WHO Reproductive Health Library and other platforms, with translations into six UN languages. Evidence briefs tailored for policymakers, program managers, and healthcare professionals will be developed in collaboration with organizations like USAID, FIGO, and ICM. 6. Interactive and User-Friendly Formats: An interactive web-based version of the guideline is planned to enhance accessibility and facilitate updates. This format will allow cross-referenced recommendations to remain current and comprehensive. 7. Support for Local Implementation: National and subnational working groups will receive support to adapt and implement the guideline. This includes revising existing national protocols, developing training manuals, and creating quality indicators tailored to local contexts. 8. Monitoring and Evaluation: The impact of the guideline will be monitored at health service, regional, and country levels. WHO’s standards for improving maternal and newborn care will guide the evaluation of quality indicators and outcomes. 9. Updating the Guideline: A systematic process will be employed to identify and address evidence gaps. 10. Research and Evidence Gaps: The WHO will continue to monitor developments in intrapartum care research, particularly in areas with limited or low-quality evidence. New recommendations or updates will be issued as warranted. 11. Global Collaboration: 12. Economic Considerations: The cost-effectiveness of interventions, including labor monitoring tools like the partograph, will be evaluated to optimize resource allocation in LMICs. 13. Respectful Maternity Care: Efforts will focus on promoting respectful care during childbirth, addressing mistreatment, and improving communication between maternity staff and women in labor. 14. Continuous Support During Labor: Evidence supports the benefits of continuous support during labor, such as the use of trained doulas, in improving maternal satisfaction and birth outcomes. 15. Labor Monitoring and Management: The use of tools like the partograph and strategies for early labor assessment will be evaluated for their effectiveness in improving maternal and neonatal outcomes. 16. Addressing Prolonged Labor: Research will explore the impact of prolonged labor on women’s experiences and outcomes, as well as interventions to prevent or manage delays in labor progression. 17. Open Access to Research: This content reflects a comprehensive approach to improving intrapartum care, emphasizing evidence-based practices, global collaboration, and respect for women’s experiences during childbirth.
